Oftentimes
OF-en-times
adv.
A compound of often and times. Webster 1828: frequently; often; many times. The Authorized Version also uses the shorter ofttimes. Its most weighty use is in Hebrews, where the repetition of a sacrifice proves its insufficiency.

Biblical Definition

Oftentimes means repeatedly, and Hebrews turns the repetition itself into an argument. And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins (Hebrews 10:11). Every word in that sentence is doing work: the priest standeth, because there was no seat in the tabernacle — his work was never finished; he offers oftentimes the same sacrifices, and a remedy that must be endlessly repeated is thereby shown not to have cured anything. Two verses later comes the contrast: But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God. Luke uses the word of a demoniac’s long torment: for oftentimes it had caught him: and he was kept bound with chains and in fetters; and he brake the bands (Luke 8:29). Paul uses it of intentions repeatedly frustrated by providence: oftentimes I purposed to come unto you, (but was let hitherto,) that I might have some fruit among you also (Romans 1:13). And Ecclesiastes uses it to disarm a man offended by gossip: oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others (Ecclesiastes 7:22).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines OFTENTIMES as frequently; often; many times; and notes the shorter form OFTTIMES with the same signification.

expand to see more

OFTENTIMES, adv. — Frequently; often; many times; again and again.

OFTTIMES, adv. — The shorter form of the same word, also used in the Authorized Version.

OFTEN, adv. — Frequently; many times; not seldom.

Compounded of often and times, the plural adding emphasis to the repetition.

From Saxon oft, often — the root also of oftener and oftenest.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 10:11 — "And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins:"

Luke 8:29 — "(For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. For oftentimes it had caught him: and he was kept bound with chains and in fetters; and he brake the bands, and was driven of the devil into the wilderness.)"

Romans 1:13 — "Now I would not have you ignorant, brethren, that oftentimes I purposed to come unto you, (but was let hitherto,) that I might have some fruit among you also, even as among other Gentiles."

Ecclesiastes 7:22 — "For oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others."

Modern Corruption

Hebrews 10:11 makes the repetition of a sacrifice the proof of its insufficiency, which is the New Testament’s own argument against the Roman doctrine of the Mass as a propitiatory offering repeated daily on thousands of altars.

expand to see more

The writer to the Hebrews builds his case on repetition. If the Levitical sacrifices had perfected the worshippers, would they not have ceased to be offered? (Hebrews 10:2). They did not cease; they were offered oftentimes, daily, standing; therefore they did not perfect anyone, and it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins. Against this stands the Roman doctrine, defined at Trent and reaffirmed since, that the Mass is a true and proper propitiatory sacrifice in which the same Christ is offered in an unbloody manner. Whatever the intention, the logic of Hebrews cuts straight through it: a sacrifice offered again is a sacrifice not finished. The contrast the chapter draws is between a priest who stands and a Priest who sat down, and the sitting is the whole argument.

Romans 1:13 offers a quieter correction. Paul purposed oftentimes to come to Rome and was hindered every time; he says so in the opening paragraph of the letter without a hint that the hindrance meant he had misread God’s will. He eventually reached Rome as a prisoner, after a shipwreck, at the empire’s expense. Repeated frustration of a good intention is not a verdict on the intention. Ecclesiastes 7:22 supplies a third and homelier use, and it is one of the wisest verses in Scripture for a wounded man: do not go looking for what people say of you, for oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek pollakis (G4178), often, frequently; chronois pollois, for a long time; Hebrew peamim rabboth, many times; Greek ephapax (G2178), once for all — the deliberate contrast in Hebrews.

expand to see more

Greek pollakis (G4178) — often, many times; offering oftentimes the same sacrifices (Hebrews 10:11).

Greek ephapax (G2178) — once for all; the word Hebrews sets against pollakis (Hebrews 7:27, 9:12, 10:10).

Greek chronos (G5550) — time, duration; ofttimes it had caught him is pollois chronois in Luke 8:29.

Hebrew peamim (H6471) — times, occurrences; oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth (Ecclesiastes 7:22).

Greek kathemeran — daily; the priest of Hebrews 10:11 stands daily ministering.

Usage

"Offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins (Hebrews 10:11) — repetition as proof of insufficiency."

"Oftentimes I purposed to come unto you, (but was let hitherto,) (Romans 1:13) — repeated hindrance is not a verdict on the intention."

"Thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others (Ecclesiastes 7:22) — the cure for listening at doors."
